behavior_items: The reproducer exercises AArch64 NEON structured load intrinsics that map to `ld2` instructions. `vld2_f32(p1)` loads two interleaved 32-bit float lanes from memory into a `float32x2x2_t`, i.e. a 2-register vector aggregate. `vld2q_f64(p1)` does the analogous operation for two 128-bit vectors of doubles.

The key semantic pattern is a two-step construction of the same vector aggregate: first load a complete 2-register structure from `p1`, then update only one lane of each register from `p2` using `vld2_lane_f32` or `vld2q_lane_f64`. Conceptually, the second intrinsic should reuse the registers holding the first load and overwrite lane 1 in place.

In `f`, the source-level logic is: load `{a0,a1}` / `{b0,b1}` from interleaved memory at `p1` into the two vectors of `v`, then replace the second element of each vector using two scalars loaded interleaved from `p2`, and finally return the resulting 2-vector aggregate in the standard AArch64 SIMD return registers.

In `f2`, the same behavior is exercised on the smaller 64-bit vector type `float32x2x2_t`. The function returns a 2-register SIMD aggregate after partially updating lane 1. This stresses not only the lane-load operation but also return-value register assignment for a small aggregate of vector registers.

In `f3`, the result is not returned directly but stored through an output pointer. This checks whether the same redundant-copy behavior appears even when the final value lives only long enough to be stored, i.e. when ABI return-register constraints are absent from the final observable result.

The emitted GCC AArch64 code shows that after the first `ld2`, GCC copies the loaded vector registers into different vector registers using `mov`, and then performs the lane `ld2` into the copied registers. For example, `f3` does `ld2 {v2.2s-v3.2s}, [x1]`, copies `v2/v3` into `v0/v1`, then executes `ld2 {v0.s-v1.s}[1], [x2]`. Since the lane load only overwrites one lane and preserves the others, these copies are functionally unnecessary if the original load had gone directly into the final destination registers.

The redundant moves appear in multiple shapes depending on register allocation. In `f`, GCC first loads into `v4/v5` and copies into return registers `v0/v1` before the lane load. In `f2`, GCC loads into `v0/v1`, copies into `v2/v3` for the lane load, then copies back into `v0/v1` for the return. In `f3`, GCC loads into `v2/v3`, copies into `v0/v1`, performs the lane load, and stores from `v0/v1`. All three variants indicate the same underlying issue: the compiler fails to keep the structured load and structured lane update on the same register pair.

The reproducer therefore is not exposing wrong-code behavior; it exposes a code-generation inefficiency. The generated code is semantically correct because the copied registers contain the same data before the lane overwrite, but the extra `mov` instructions increase instruction count and potentially register pressure.

The lane form of `ld2` is especially important here because it is a read-modify-write style vector operation at the architectural level: it loads only one specified lane of each destination register and leaves the remaining lanes unchanged. That makes direct reuse of the destination registers from the prior `ld2` the ideal lowering, exactly as shown by Clang and by GCC on AArch32.

The bug is AArch64-specific in the report because other compilers/targets are able to preserve the same register tuple across both operations. Clang on AArch64 emits the minimal sequence: initial `ld2` into the final registers, lane `ld2` into the same registers, then `ret` or store. GCC on AArch32 likewise keeps the same D-register pair live across both instructions.

The reproducer also demonstrates that the inefficiency is optimization-level insensitive across the tested levels (`-O1`, `-O2`, `-O3`, `-Ofast`, `-Os`). That suggests the missed optimization is not a late peephole opportunity only, but more likely stems from target-specific expansion, RTL constraints, or register-tuple handling for AArch64 Advanced SIMD structure loads and lane loads.

A likely compiler-internal stress point is the representation of multi-register SIMD aggregates and tuple constraints. `ld2` and `ld2_lane` require a consecutive register pair, and the compiler appears to materialize the first intrinsic and second intrinsic as separate values that are not coalesced onto the same hard-register tuple. The result is copy insertion before or after the lane load to satisfy tuple placement and calling-convention/storage requirements.

The fact that `-Os` still keeps the moves is especially informative: GCC is not merely trading code size for some perceived scheduling benefit. Instead, it likely believes the copies are structurally required by its chosen operand allocation or by how the intrinsics are expanded, even though better coalescing is clearly possible.

`f3` is the cleanest minimal case for understanding the exercised behavior: `v = vld2_f32(p1);` creates a pair of scalar-lane vectors from interleaved memory, `vld2_lane_f32(p2, v, 1)` updates lane 1 of each vector using a second interleaved load, and `*p = ...;` stores the finished pair. An optimal backend can map that directly to one `ld2`, one lane `ld2`, and one `stp`/store pair with no register copies at all.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer targets GCC AArch64 NEON code generation for structured loads followed by structured lane loads on the same vector tuple. Source code first builds a 2-register SIMD aggregate with `vld2_*`, then updates one lane of each register with `vld2_*_lane`, either returning the aggregate or storing it. Because lane loads preserve untouched lanes, the optimal lowering is to perform both instructions on the same destination register pair. Clang and GCC AArch32 do exactly that. GCC AArch64 instead inserts extra `mov` instructions to copy the tuple between register pairs before and/or after the lane load, depending on the function. The generated code is correct but unnecessarily longer and creates extra register pressure, showing an AArch64-specific missed coalescing/expansion optimization for NEON structure-load tuple registers rather than a semantic miscompile.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is an AArch64 Advanced SIMD/NEON tuple operation sequence where a full structured load (`ld2`) is immediately followed by a lane structured load (`ld2 ...[lane]`) into the same logical 2-register aggregate. The observed failure is not wrong code but a target-specific code-generation inefficiency: GCC fails to preserve/coalesce the original tuple registers across these two operations, so it inserts register-to-register `mov` copies before and/or after the lane load. This happens for both 64-bit and 128-bit vector tuples, for both return and store cases, and across all optimization levels including `-Os`, which strongly suggests the root problem is in AArch64 backend lowering, operand constraints, or register allocation for consecutive SIMD register tuples rather than in generic optimization. The likely defect class is mishandling of read-modify-write semantics of `ld2_lane` and poor coalescing of multi-register NEON aggregate values, causing GCC to believe a different hard-register pair is required for the lane update or final ABI placement.
possible_causes: AArch64 NEON intrinsic expansion for `vld2_*` and `vld2_*_lane` does not preserve the same logical register tuple across both operations, causing unnecessary copies between consecutive SIMD register pairs.

The backend patterns/constraints for AArch64 `ld2` lane instructions likely model the destination tuple too rigidly or as a separate value, preventing direct reuse of the registers produced by the preceding structured load.

Register allocation or reload for AArch64 consecutive SIMD tuple operands is failing to coalesce producer and consumer of a 2-register aggregate, so copy insertion occurs to satisfy tuple-register placement constraints.
The AArch64 backend may be mishandling the read-modify-write nature of `ld2_lane`, treating it like it needs a fresh destination tuple instead of updating the already-loaded tuple in place.

Return-value handling for small SIMD aggregates on AArch64 may interact badly with tuple register allocation, especially in functions returning `float32x2x2_t`/`float64x2x2_t`, leading to copies into or out of ABI return registers.

AArch64 target-specific combine/peephole optimization is missing for the pattern `ld2` followed by `ld2_lane` on the same tuple, so redundant `mov` instructions introduced earlier are never eliminated.

The machine description or expander for structured lane loads may not express tied operands or early enough hard-register preferences for consecutive vector registers, forcing later copy-based repair.

There may be an AArch64-specific deficiency in handling multi-register SIMD aggregates in RTL (parallel/consecutive register tuples), unlike AArch32, leading to failure to keep the tuple live in one register pair through the whole sequence.
evidence: All examples show the same source pattern: first `vld2_*` builds a 2-register vector aggregate, then `vld2_*_lane` updates one lane of that same aggregate.
The generated AArch64 code is semantically correct but contains extra `mov` instructions around the lane `ld2`, proving the issue is redundant copying rather than incorrect computation.

The redundancy appears in multiple forms: load into one pair then copy to return regs (`f`), load into return regs then copy to another pair then back (`f2`), and load into one pair then copy to store regs (`f3`). This points to a common tuple-register allocation/coalescing problem.
`ld2 ...[lane]` preserves untouched lanes, so if the first `ld2` had been emitted directly into the final tuple registers, no copies would be needed.
Clang on AArch64 emits the optimal sequence with no `mov`, showing the architecture and ABI do not require those copies.
GCC on AArch32 also keeps the same register pair across structured load and lane update, so the problem is specific to GCC's AArch64 backend rather than to the intrinsic semantics.
The issue occurs for both 64-bit and 128-bit vector tuple types, indicating it is not tied to a single mode size but to the general handling of NEON structured tuple loads.

The issue persists from `-O1` through `-O3`, `-Ofast`, and `-Os`, suggesting the root cause is in target-specific lowering/constraints/register allocation rather than a missed high-level optimization pass.

selected_files.reason: Most suspicious because the bug is AArch64-specific and involves NEON structured load plus lane-load instruction selection (`ld2` and `ld2 ...[lane]`). These tuple operations and their operand tying/consecutive-register constraints are typically defined in the AArch64 SIMD machine description, so redundant copies are likely caused by incorrect patterns, expanders, or missing tied/coalescing-friendly constraints there.

The reproducer uses AArch64 NEON intrinsics (`vld2_*`, `vld2_*_lane`) directly. Their builtin expansion may be creating separate values for the initial structure load and lane update instead of preserving one read-modify-write tuple, which would naturally force extra moves before/after RTL matching.

`ld2`/`ld2_lane` require consecutive SIMD register tuples. If the AArch64 constraint definitions are too rigid or fail to express the desired same-register-pair reuse, reload/LRA may introduce compensating moves exactly like those seen in the output.

Predicates used by the AArch64 SIMD patterns can influence whether the compiler recognizes and matches tuple register operands directly. An overly restrictive or mismatched predicate for structured lane loads could prevent reuse of the original tuple registers and trigger copy insertion.

This file contains target ABI and register-handling logic for AArch64. Since the issue appears both in returned SIMD aggregates and stored ones, and differs across functions depending on final register placement, AArch64 target hooks related to composite/vector aggregate handling or hard-register preferences may be contributing to the missed coalescing.

If the machine description already describes the operations reasonably, the next likely culprit is LRA constraint processing. The observed copies look like constraint-repair moves inserted to satisfy consecutive tuple-register requirements for `ld2_lane`, suggesting LRA may be failing to keep producer and consumer on one register pair.

The extra `mov` instructions persist even at `-Os`, which suggests GCC fails to eliminate structurally unnecessary copies after allocation. A weakness in LRA-side coalescing for multi-register SIMD tuples could leave exactly these redundant register-pair copies in place.

This pass propagates hard-register copies and can remove redundant copy chains after reload. Since the generated code shows obvious same-value vector moves around the lane load, insufficient handling of multi-register SIMD tuple copies here could explain why the moves survive to final output.

A register-renaming deficiency could prevent the backend from renaming the first `ld2` destination tuple to the final tuple used by the lane load and return/store. That would leave unnecessary moves in otherwise valid code, especially for consecutive SIMD register pairs.

Least likely among the top suspects, but still relevant because final can suppress unnecessary moves after good allocation. If these copies are technically distinct hard-register moves yet semantically dead due to tied tuple usage, missing final-stage elimination could be why they remain visible in the emitted assembly.

The register allocator chooses POINTER_AND_FP_REGS if FP_REGS and GENERAL_REGS have the same cost - even if POINTER_AND_FP_REGS has a much higher cost. POINTER_AND_FP_REGS is also used if the cost of both FP_REGS and GENERAL_REGS is lower than the memory cost (in this case the best class is the lowest cost one). Using POINTER_AND_FP_REGS irrespectively of its cost results in bad allocations with many redundant int<->FP moves which are expensive on various cores. To avoid this we don't allow POINTER_AND_FP_REGS as the allocno class, but force a decision between FP_REGS and GENERAL_REGS. We use the allocno class if it isn't POINTER_AND_FP_REGS. Similarly, use the best class if it isn't POINTER_AND_FP_REGS. Otherwise set the allocno class depending on the mode. The result of this is that it is no longer inefficient to have a higher memory move cost than the register move cost.

For example: (set (reg:VNx8HI R1) (subreg:VNx8HI (reg:VNx16QI R2) 0)) represents a VIEW_CONVERT between the following vectors, viewed in memory order: R2: { [0].high, [0].low, [1].high, [1].low, ... } R1: { [0], [1], [2], [3], ... } The high part of lane X in R2 should therefore correspond to lane X*2 of R1, but the register representations are: msb lsb R2: ......
